sources: Missouri Department of Conservation, Field Guide: Wolf Spiders: a row of four small eyes below the four larger ones; at night, shine a flashlight held beside your eyes and their eyes shine back at you like a cat's; they do not spin webs, they run prey down; the female attaches her egg sac to her spinnerets and later carries her babies on her back; body length 1/4 inch to 1 inch depending on species; North American wolf spider bites are harmless; https://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/wolf-spiders

Penn State Extension, Wolf Spiders: bite if mishandled or trapped next to the skin; initial pain and redness, possibly localized swelling, subsiding within 24 hours; no serious medical consequences of these bites have been noted; females commonly carry their young on their backs in summer; build retreats in soil and under objects and come out at night to look for prey; fertilized females overwinter in protected places including human-made structures; Hogna carolinensis females 22-35 mm long; https://extension.psu.edu/wolf-spiders

Montana State University Extension, Spiders of Montana: Wolf Spiders: hunting spiders that do not build webs to catch prey; excellent vision used for prey capture; females attach egg sacs to their spinnerets; hatched spiderlings stay on the mother's abdomen until ready to disperse; https://urbanipm.montana.edu/entomology/resources/fact-sheets/spiders_of_montana/wolf.spiders.html

University of California Statewide IPM Program, Pest Notes: Black Widow and Other Widow Spiders (general spider section): most spiders have venom which they use to kill their prey; https://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/PESTNOTES/pn7442.html
UC Riverside, Rick Vetter, How to Identify (and Misidentify) a Brown Recluse Spider: recluses have six eyes in three pairs, while most spiders have eight; https://spiders.ucr.edu/recluseid.html

beats.say: A big spider is running across your floor, with its back covered in babies.
Turn off the lights, shine a flashlight, and its eyes glow back at you, like a cat's.
The wolf spider. No web. It runs its prey down.
Venomous? Yes. Most spiders have venom, to kill its prey.
But it only bites if you grab it, or trap it against your skin.
The bite hurts, and goes red. But it fades within a day.
How to tell it's a wolf spider? Four small eyes in a row, under four big ones.
Scary to look at. Harmless to you. And a really good mom.
First, the mom carries her egg sac, stuck to the tip of her body.
When the babies hatch, they ride on her back, until they can live on their own.
Some kinds are big. A female Carolina wolf spider can be well over an inch long.
By day, it hides in the soil, and under rocks and logs.
At night, it comes out to hunt, with excellent eyesight.
In the fall, some females move into buildings, to spend the winter.
But don't mix it up with a brown recluse.
A recluse has only six eyes, in three pairs. Most spiders have eight.
Would you let a wolf spider live in your garage?
